3.text: without any watch; and two boys are sufficient to keep watch for several

4.text: weeks, with an occasional visit from their father or elder brother, who attend

5.text: chiefly to the change of pasture. Thus in the winter-time the older people

6.text: have more leisure for visits and amusements.

7.text: The Chukchee are supplied with meat and skins from their herds. No

8.text: milking is possible on account of the wildness of the reindeer. Early in summer

9.text: the herdsmen may catch one of the does with fawn, strike her to the ground,

10.text: and try to suck some milk from her udder, although she may kick desperately

11.text: all the while. The man has to strike her udder with his fist, just as the fawn

12.text: does with its forehead, to cause a more abundant flow of milk. Sometimes

13.text: the milk that has been sucked out is spit into a bladder and brought home

14.text: as a rare present. The amount is rarely more than half a glassful. But these

15.text: milking-operations must not be repeated too frequently, otherwise the fawn

16.text: would be starved. When the herdsman is very hungry, he may also chop

17.text: off a few pieces of the soft velvet of some buck with large antlers, and eat

18.text: the thick, soft outer skin. The animal is released without any dressing of the

19.text: wound; and the blood will sometimes continue to trickle down for hours.

20.text: Bucks are gelded in a way somewhat corresponding to the process of

21.text: milking. The animal is struck to the ground, and the herdsman bites with

22.text: his teeth either through the dowcets or through the spermatic ducts. This

23.text: operation does not affect the reindeer much, and immediately afterward it

24.text: continues to graze. Sometimes the scrotum is tied very tightly with a sinew

25.text: thread, and after a while becomes atrophied and drops off. Usually the antlers

26.text: of the driving-reindeer are cut short with a saw early in the fall, when they
